Hook: The mathematician Stanislaw Ulam was one of the inventors of the Monte Carlo method. One day he put a challenge to his friend Paul Samuelson, who would become the first American to win the Nobel prize in economics. Name me one proposition in all of the social sciences, he said, which is both true and not trivial. Samuelson had no answer that day.

Years later, as Samuelson told it, he had his answer: David Ricardo's theory of comparative advantage. That it is logically true, he said, need not be argued before a mathematician. That it is not trivial is attested by the thousands of important and intelligent men who have never been able to grasp the doctrine for themselves, or to believe it after it was explained to them. This part is about that idea, what it gets right and what it leaves out: above all, that trade makes a country richer without making everyone in it richer.

And it matters more than ever. Here is trade, exports plus imports, as a share of output in eighteen rich economies since 1870. In the median economy it was 33 percent in 1870 and 42 percent by 1913, the first globalization. Then two wars and a depression: by 1932 it was down to 25 percent. It took until the 1970s to recover, and by 2019 it was 60 percent. America, a continent that trades mostly with itself, went from 5 percent in 1932 to 26 percent.

This part's question: why do countries trade, and who wins and loses when they do? Why does a country that is worse at making everything still have something to sell? What do a country's endowments, its labour, capital and land, decide about what it trades? And who loses, why do the losers so often win in politics, and could the winners pay them?
Economics, Built. Part thirty-five: trade, and comparative advantage.

Here is the plan. A game with four numbers, then Ricardo's own, then many goods, and a test: Japan, opened to trade under American naval pressure in the 1850s. A second theory, in which what a country has decides what it sells, its theorems about who loses, and the paradox and the puzzle that its tests turned up. Who loses first, and what a tariff does. Why protection is for sale, why countries sign trade agreements, and whether the winners can pay the losers. And a new dial: how much a country gains from trade.
PlayIt: Chapter one. Play it: four numbers.

Your turn. The Island and its neighbour, the Archipelago, make two things: fish and cloth. Here are the hours of work each needs for one unit. The Island needs three hours to land a fish and six to weave a bolt of cloth. The Archipelago, with better boats and better looms, needs one hour for a fish and four for a bolt. The Archipelago is better at both. The Island has twice as many hours of work to offer each week, and people in both spend half their income on fish and half on cloth.

If they trade, who should make what? Should the Archipelago make both, since it is better at both? Should the Island make the cloth and the Archipelago the fish? Or the other way round? Pause, and choose.

The answer is B, and the reason is in what each good costs in terms of the other. On the Island, the six hours that weave a bolt of cloth could land two fish; so a bolt costs two fish. In the Archipelago, four hours of weaving could land four fish: a bolt costs four. Cloth is relatively cheap on the Island. That is its comparative advantage, even though it is worse at weaving in absolute terms. Here is what each can make alone: its production frontier, and the white dot, what it consumes with half its income on each good. Now let them trade at a price between the two costs, 3 fish a bolt, which is where the market settles. The Island weaves only cloth and sells half of it for fish; the Archipelago fishes only, and buys cloth. Each can now reach the dashed line, beyond its own frontier. The Island consumes the same cloth and half as much fish again; the Archipelago the same fish and a third more cloth: gains of 22 and 15 percent, for both, from the same hours of work.

One more number. After trade an Islander earns half a fish an hour, and an Archipelagan 1 fish: the Island's wage is half the Archipelago's, because its workers are less productive. So both sides have a fear. In the Archipelago people say they cannot compete with the Island's cheap labour. On the Island people say they cannot compete with the Archipelago's better boats and looms. Both are wrong. Wages follow productivity, trade follows comparative cost, and the gains go to both.
Ricardo: In 1817 David Ricardo, a stockbroker who had made a fortune and turned to economics, put the idea in four numbers. England needs the labour of a hundred men for a year to make a certain quantity of cloth, and a hundred and twenty to make a quantity of wine. Portugal needs ninety and eighty. Portugal is better at both. Yet in England a unit of wine costs the labour of one point two units of cloth, and in Portugal under nine tenths. Wine is relatively cheap in Portugal and cloth in England, and that, Ricardo argued, decides the trade.

Let them trade. The world's supply of wine relative to cloth is a staircase. At any price below Portugal's own cost, under nine tenths of a unit of cloth, nobody makes wine. At Portugal's cost, Portugal will make any amount. Between the two costs, Portugal makes only wine and England only cloth, and at England's cost England starts making wine too. The world's demand slopes down. If England has a quarter more workers than Portugal, the two meet at a price of one unit of cloth for a unit of wine, between the two costs, and each country makes only its cheaper good. Now England gets a unit of wine for the labour of a hundred men instead of a hundred and twenty, and Portugal gets cloth for eighty instead of ninety. Both save labour. In consumption, England gains 6 percent and Portugal 10.

What do workers earn? Portugal's wage must be higher than England's, since its workers are more productive at both; but not too much higher. If it were less than a hundred over ninety times England's, Portugal could undersell England's cloth too. If it were more than a hundred and twenty over eighty, England could undersell Portugal's wine. In between, where demand puts it, here at 1.25, each country sells what it is relatively good at. A country with low productivity competes through low wages; a country with high productivity can afford high ones. Ricardo's insight is that it is relative, not absolute, cost that decides who sells what.
Many: Chapter three. Many goods: the chain and the continuum.

With two goods the answer is a comparison. With many it is a chain. Rank the goods by how much more productive the Island is than the Archipelago at each, its relative edge. Now draw the Island's wage relative to the Archipelago's. The Island makes every good whose edge is larger than its relative wage, and buys the rest. Where the line falls depends on wages, and wages depend on demand: if the line were too high, the Island would sell too little and its wage would fall.

In 1977 Rudiger Dornbusch, Stanley Fischer and Paul Samuelson took the chain to its limit: a continuum of goods, lined up from the Island's strongest to its weakest. The teal curve is the Island's edge along the line, falling. The gold curve is demand: if the Island makes every good up to some point, the relative wage at which its exports pay for its imports. The more goods it makes, the more the world spends on them, and the higher that wage. They cross at a relative wage of 0.78, with the Island making 28 percent of the goods. Two curves, and the whole pattern of trade and wages follows.

The model earns its keep in experiments. Let the Archipelago's workforce grow by half. Its demand for the Island's goods rises, and the gold curve shifts up. The Island's relative wage rises, from 0.78 to 0.90, and it gives up its marginal industries to the Archipelago: it makes 23 percent of goods instead of 28. Losing industries and gaining income at the same time is what the theory predicts. Now add the cost of shipping: suppose 15 percent of a cargo is lost on the way. A good is exported only if the edge beats the wage by enough to pay for the trip, so the edge curve splits in two, and between them lies a band of goods, 11 percent here, that each country makes for itself: haircuts, houses, most services.
Japan: Chapter four. A test: Japan opens.

Comparative advantage is hard to test, because it is about prices a country would have had without trade, and almost no country is ever seen without trade. Japan is the exception. From 1639 it allowed almost no foreign trade. In 1853 Commodore Matthew Perry's American warships arrived, and the treaties that followed opened its ports in July 1859, with tariffs capped at low rates. Daniel Bernhofen and John Brown saw a natural experiment: prices from the last years of isolation, 1851 to 1853, are recorded, and the opening was sudden, nearly complete, and not Japan's choice.

What did Japan trade? It exported silk, silkworm eggs and tea: those three were four fifths of its exports. It imported woollens, cotton cloth and yarn, sugar and rice: the products of Lancashire's mills and of tropical plantations. And prices moved as the theory says they should when a country joins the world market: those of its exports, silk above all, rose, some almost doubling relative to other prices; those of its imports fell.

Now the test. The theory makes a sharp prediction: value a country's net exports at the prices it had before trade, and the total must be negative, since it sells what was cheap at home and buys what was dear. Here are Japan's exports in each year from 1868 to 1875, valued at the prices of 1851 to 1853, and its imports at the same prices: at the old prices, its exports are worth less than its imports. The total is negative in all 8 years: in 1875, minus 8.1 million ryo. A two hundred year old theory, tested against a natural experiment, and it passes.

How much did Japan gain? In a second paper Bernhofen and Brown put an upper bound on the static gain: no more than 8 or 9 percent of GDP. The reverse experiment gives a similar number. In December 1807 President Jefferson banned American ships from foreign trade, an embargo that lasted until March 1809. Douglas Irwin estimates its cost at about 5 percent of national income. Real, but not enormous. The gains from comparative advantage are triangles: they depend on how much a country trades and how different its prices were. Part thirty-six adds gains that are not triangles: from scale, variety and the best firms growing.
HO: Ricardo explains trade by differences in technology. In 1919 the Swedish economist Eli Heckscher, and in 1933 his student Bertil Ohlin, offered a second reason, which needs no difference in technology at all. Give every country the same ways of making things, and let them differ only in what they have. The Island has many workers and little capital; the Archipelago has fewer workers and much more capital. And the two goods use them in different proportions: weaving cloth takes mostly labour, building machines mostly capital.

The model has a picture, drawn by Abba Lerner as a student in 1933. The pink curve is every mix of labour and capital that makes one dollar's worth of cloth at world prices. The blue curve, one dollar's worth of machines: it lies up and to the left, because machines need more capital. If both are made, each must cost exactly a dollar to make, so a single line of inputs costing one dollar must touch both curves. That line fixes the wage and the rent. The prices of goods determine the prices of the factors, whatever a country's endowments, which is the first surprising result. The two dashed rays are the proportions each good uses; a country with endowments between them makes both goods.

Now let the two trade. Alone, the Island, short of capital, finds machines dear: 1.42 bolts of cloth each. The Archipelago, rich in capital, pays 0.82. With trade one price settles between them, 1.04, and the Island sells 42 bolts of cloth for 41 machines. That is the Heckscher-Ohlin theorem: a country exports the good that uses its abundant factor intensively. And something stranger happens. Labour on the Island, cheap before trade, gets dearer; capital gets cheaper; and the wage and the rent end up exactly the same in both places, though not one worker or machine has crossed the sea. Trading goods is a way of trading the labour and capital inside them.

Four theorems come out of this picture. Heckscher and Ohlin's, about the pattern of trade. Factor price equalization, the one we just saw. Stolper and Samuelson's, about who gains, which is the next chapter. And Rybczynski's: at fixed prices, more capital raises the output of machines by more than its own growth and lowers the output of cloth. Give the Archipelago ten percent more capital and it makes 13 percent more machines and 34 percent less cloth. Growth can make an economy more specialized, not less.
Stolper: Chapter six. Stolper and Samuelson: losers inside.

In 1941 Wolfgang Stolper and Paul Samuelson asked who gains from trade inside a country. Hold the price of machines fixed and raise the price of cloth, the labour-intensive good. The wage rises, and the rent on capital falls. It has to: both goods must still just cover their costs, and cloth's costs are mostly wages, so for cloth to earn exactly its higher price while machines earn the same old one, labour must get more and capital less.

The effect is magnified. Raise the price of cloth by ten percent, leaving machines alone. The wage rises by 18 percent, more than either price, and the rent falls by 7 percent. So workers can buy more of both goods, and capital owners less of both, whatever they like to consume. There is no ambiguity about who wins.

Now open the two economies to each other. On the Island, where labour is abundant, trade raises the price of cloth, its export: workers gain and capital owners lose. In the Archipelago it is the other way round: its workers lose to the Island's competition and its capital owners gain. That is the theorem's political content: trade makes a country richer and, in this model, makes its scarce factor poorer, unambiguously. Surveys in rich countries, where less-skilled labour is the scarce factor, find what the theorem suggests: less-skilled workers are more likely to favour limits on imports than skilled ones.
Leontief: Chapter seven. Leontief's paradox, and the missing trade.

The first serious test of Heckscher and Ohlin came in 1953, from Wassily Leontief, who had built the input-output table of Part three. He asked how much capital and labour it would take to make a million dollars of America's exports, counting everything that goes into them, and a million dollars of the goods America imported, if America had to make them itself. Per worker-year, the exports needed about fourteen thousand dollars of capital; the import replacements about eighteen thousand. The richest country in capital in the world, in 1947, was exporting labour-intensive goods and importing capital-intensive ones. The opposite of the theory.

The paradox drew answers for decades. American workers were more skilled than most; count their skill as a kind of capital, and the exports look intensive in it. Many imports were raw materials that need land, mines or climate America lacked. Leontief's own answer was that American workers were so productive that, counted in efficiency units, labour was America's abundant factor. And in 1980 Edward Leamer showed that with unbalanced trade, as America's was in 1947, Leontief's comparison is the wrong test; the right one, comparing what the country produces with what it consumes, shows America abundant in capital after all.

The modern test uses every factor and every country at once. In 1995 Daniel Trefler took thirty-three countries and nine factors, kinds of labour, capital and land, in 1983. For each, the theory predicts how much of the factor a country's trade should carry, from how much of it the country has compared with its share of world spending. If the theory held, every point would sit on the dashed line. Instead, recomputed here from Trefler's own data, the measured content has the right sign 50 percent of the time, no better than a coin. And the points lie almost flat: the measured factor content has about 38 times less variance than the prediction. Trefler called it the case of the missing trade. His remedy, and Donald Davis and David Weinstein's after him, was to let technology differ across countries, as Ricardo had, and to let people prefer goods made at home. With both, the theory fits far better. Ricardo and Heckscher and Ohlin are not rivals: real trade needs both.
Specific: Chapter eight. Specific factors: who loses first.

Heckscher and Ohlin's world is a long run, in which capital moves freely between industries. Tomorrow, a loom cannot plough a field. The specific-factors model, set out by Ronald Jones and Paul Samuelson in 1971, takes that seriously: labour moves, but capital is stuck in manufacturing and land in farming. The gold curve is what a worker adds in the factories, with workers counted from the left; the brown curve what a worker adds on the farms, counted from the right. Workers move until the two are equal, and that sets the wage. Now the price of food rises 10 percent. The farm curve shifts up, workers move to the farms, and the wage rises, but only 5 percent, less than the price of food. Landowners gain 15 percent; the owners of factories lose 5. And workers? Better off in manufactures, worse off in food: it depends on what they eat.

This is why trade politics looks the way it does. The losers from imports are few and concentrated: the owners and workers of one industry, often in one region. A tariff on cloth is worth a great deal to each weaver and each mill owner. It costs each shopper a little, perhaps too little to notice. Mancur Olson explained in 1965 why that matters: small groups with large stakes organize, lobby and vote on the issue; large groups with small stakes do not. So trade policy tends to be made by and for the specific factors, which is the starting point of chapter ten.
Tariff: Now the tool most often used to change trade: the tariff. Here is the Island's market for cloth: demand in white, the Island's own weavers' supply in gold. At the world price of 4, Islanders buy 60 bolts a week and weave 20; the other 40 are imported. A tariff of 1 raises the price at home to 5. Islanders buy less, weave more, and imports halve. Shoppers lose 55: everything between the two prices, left of demand. Weavers gain 25 of it, the gold area. The treasury collects 20, the blue rectangle. And the two red triangles, 10 in all, go to no one: cloth woven at home at more than it costs abroad, and cloth not bought that was worth more to buyers than it cost the world. A small country that taxes imports makes itself poorer.

A quota does the same to prices with a different owner. Limit imports to 20 bolts and the price rises to 5, as with the tariff. But the blue rectangle is no longer tax revenue. It goes to whoever holds the right to import, and if that is foreign exporters, the Island loses it too. From 1981 Japan's car makers agreed to limit their exports to America, at America's request. American buyers paid more for Japanese cars, and much of the difference went to the Japanese firms.

There is one case in which a tariff can pay. Suppose the Island is large, a big enough buyer that when it buys less, the world price falls. Then part of the tariff is paid by foreigners: the Archipelago's weavers now receive 3.75 a bolt instead of 4. The green curve is the Island's gain. A small tariff helps; the best one is 0.75, about 20 percent, equal to one over the elasticity of the Archipelago's export supply, as Charles Bickerdike showed in 1906. Beyond it, the triangles win again. But every unit of that gain is a loss to the neighbour, who can play the same game. Which is the subject of chapter eleven.
Politics: If tariffs usually make a country poorer, why are there so many? History offers a clue. After 1815 Britain's Corn Laws kept out foreign grain, raising rents for the landowners who sat in Parliament, as specific factors predict. They were repealed in 1846, after a long campaign by manufacturers who wanted cheaper bread for their workers, and cheaper workers. In 1930 the United States passed the Smoot-Hawley tariff, which raised duties on thousands of goods as Congress traded votes among industries. In both, protection followed the interests that were organized, not the interest of the country.

Smoot-Hawley's reputation is worse than its arithmetic, but the arithmetic is bad enough. The average duty on America's dutiable imports rose from 40 percent in 1929 to 59 percent in 1932. Douglas Irwin has shown that much of the rise came not from the law but from deflation: many duties were so many cents a pound, and as prices fell they became a larger share of the price. Other countries retaliated, and here is the result: trade, white for the median rich economy and blue for America, fell much further than output in the early 1930s. Tariffs did not cause the Depression, but they deepened the collapse of trade. By 1948, after a decade of agreements, America's average was 14 percent.

In 1994 Gene Grossman and Elhanan Helpman turned this into a theory: protection for sale. Industries that organize offer politicians contributions in exchange for tariffs; the government weighs the contributions against the welfare of voters. The result is a formula for every industry's tariff. Organized industries get protection, more where their output is large relative to imports, so the stakes are big, and where imports respond little to price, so the triangles are small. Unorganized industries get nothing, here even a tiny subsidy to imports. How much depends on how much the government cares about welfare. If welfare counts 50 times as much as a dollar of contributions, the highest tariff on the Island is 7 percent; if only five times as much, 167 percent. Penny Goldberg and Giovanni Maggi fitted the model to American tariffs in 1983. The pattern fit, and the weight on welfare came out between 50 and 88 times that on contributions: protection is for sale, but not cheaply.
Agreements: Chapter eleven. Trade agreements: escaping a dilemma.

The large-country tariff makes trade policy a game. Two large economies, the Island and the Archipelago, each choose free trade or the tariff that is best for itself. The numbers are each country's gain over free trade, computed from Agora's model. If the Island taxes and the Archipelago does not, the Island gains 46 and the Archipelago loses 81. The reverse, in the other corner. So whatever the other does, each does better with a tariff, and both end up taxing, each 35 worse off than under free trade. It is the prisoner's dilemma of Part eleven, and the 1930s played it.

The same game as a picture. The teal line is the Island's best tariff for each tariff the Archipelago might set; the gold line, the Archipelago's. In this model the lines are straight: each country's best tariff does not depend on the other's at all, so taxing is a dominant strategy. They cross at 0.83 each, the equilibrium of a trade war, where neither wants to change. Both would be better off at the corner, with no tariffs, but neither will move there alone, because each tariff's gain comes out of the other's pocket.

Kyle Bagwell and Robert Staiger argued in 1999 that this is what trade agreements are for. In 1947 twenty-three countries signed the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, binding their tariffs and cutting them, round after round. Its rule of reciprocity means each country gives up its terms-of-trade gain at the same time as the others give up theirs. Its rule of the most favoured nation, one tariff for every member, stops two countries from striking deals that push the cost onto a third. In 1995 the World Trade Organization added a court for disputes, and permission to retaliate when a ruling is ignored. The game has not gone away. America's average tariff on goods was 2.6 percent in 2024 and 8.0 percent in 2025, the largest rise in a single year since this series begins, in 1929. Part sixty-six returns to it.
Compensation: Go back to the specific-factors Island and open it to the world, so that imported food is twenty percent cheaper. In real terms, landowners lose about a fifth of their income. Factory owners gain about a quarter, and workers a little. Add it up in money: the winners gain 9.2, the losers lose 7.4. The difference, 1.8, is the Island's gain from trade, and it is positive, as it must be: the economy can now consume a bundle it could not make. So the winners could compensate the losers in full and still be better off. In 1939 Nicholas Kaldor and John Hicks proposed that test as the meaning of an efficient change.

But could is not would. What economics shows is that opening to trade raises total income, so the winners could compensate the losers and still be ahead. The step to saying the Island should open needs a value judgment: either that a gain that could be shared is enough, whether or not it is; or that the losers will in fact be compensated; or that their loss weighs no more than someone else's gain. Part eighteen showed that economics cannot make that choice for us. It can tell us whether compensation happens.

America has tried. In 1962, in the same law that launched a round of tariff cuts, Congress created trade adjustment assistance: retraining, relocation allowances and longer unemployment benefits for workers who lose their jobs to imports. It has always been small, and many eligible workers never apply. Where it reaches people it seems to work: Benjamin Hyman, comparing workers whose cases happened to go to stricter or more lenient investigators, found that approved workers earned about 50,000 dollars more over the next 10 years. But the biggest trade shock of recent times, the surge of imports from China after 2000, fell on particular towns, and most of its losers were never compensated. That is where Part thirty-six begins.
Dials: Chapter thirteen. The Dials: the gains from trade.

How large are the gains from trade for a country today? In 2012 Costas Arkolakis, Arnaud Costinot and Andres Rodriguez-Clare showed that in a whole family of models, the answer needs only two numbers. The share of spending that goes on goods made at home, and the trade elasticity, how strongly trade responds to its costs, which gravity studies put between five and ten. For America in 2025, imports were 14 percent of GDP, so roughly 0.86 of spending stayed at home. Moving to autarky would cost between 1.5 and 2.9 percent of real income. This is rough, since GDP is not total spending; the authors' own figure, from a domestic share of 0.93, was 0.7 to 1.4 percent.

That opens a new dial: the gains from trade. Japan's opening in 1859, by Bernhofen and Brown's upper bound: eight or nine percent of GDP. America's embargo of 1807, by Irwin's estimate: about five percent. America around 2000, by the formula: under one and a half percent. And this part's rough update for today. The status: depends on the setting. Static gains from comparative advantage are a few percent of income; the models of Part thirty-six, with many sectors, intermediate goods and firms that differ, raise them.

One of the series' facts begins here, as a puzzle. Rich countries mostly trade similar goods with each other. In 2025 America exported 713 billion dollars of capital goods and imported 1133 billion; the Grubel-Lloyd index of two-way trade is 0.77. In 1967, two years after its auto pact with Canada, its car trade scored 0.93. Nothing in this part explains that: Ricardo and Heckscher and Ohlin predict trade in different goods, between countries that differ. Agora's column is empty until Part thirty-six.
Frontier: Chapter fifteen. Frontier: testing Ricardo in the fields.

Ricardo's theory is about productivity in goods a country does not make, which is why it is hard to test. You see how good Portugal is at wine, but not how good it would be at cloth if it tried. In agriculture, Arnaud Costinot and Dave Donaldson found a way round it. Agronomists at the Food and Agriculture Organization model how much of each crop any plot of land could yield, given its soil and climate, whether or not the crop is grown there: 17 crops, 1.6 million plots, 55 countries. Feed those productivities into a Ricardian model, predict what each country should grow, and compare with what it does grow: the slope is 0.21, far from one but clearly positive. Comparative advantage, measured where it can be, has real explanatory power.

The open questions. In 2002 Jonathan Eaton and Samuel Kortum turned Ricardo into a model of many countries, each drawing its productivity in each good at random; it is the engine of Part thirty-six. How large the gains are once there are many sectors and goods traded as inputs. How fast comparative advantage changes, and whether policy can change it, the question of industrial policy in Part sixty-six. Who inside a country gains, and how long adjustment takes. And trade in services and in tasks, which the old theories were not built for.
